title: Linux dev machines,
*declared in one file*
on your Mac
hero.lead: LimaNix runs NixOS virtual machines. Pick a shell, toolchains and services in `limanix.toml`, and LimaNix builds the machine and keeps it that way.

demo.label: Creating a VM from limanix.toml and opening a shell in it

features.title: Everything a project needs, nothing it does not
features.lead: A few lines of `limanix.toml` turn into tools you use every day.

items.title: A terminal that is ready
items.text: Zsh with the Pure prompt, AstroNvim, tmux, Lazygit and Yazi, all in one theme.

items.title: Your languages, wired in
items.text: Pick the languages and versions a project needs. Each comes with its build tools and a language server already connected to the editor.

items.title: Services and packages
items.text: Docker, PostgreSQL and more from the catalog, plus any package from nixpkgs or nixos-unstable.

items.title: Your project, shared with the VM
items.text: Code stays on the Mac and appears in the VM as you edit it. Share any folder, read-write or read-only.

items.title: Your dotfiles, in every VM
items.text: Name the folder with your dotfiles once. Every new shell links them into the home, and edits on the Mac apply at once.

items.title: Answers inside the VM
items.text: `lmx` shows how the VM is doing, what is wrong and what to do, and what each module can do.
code: $ lmx status       # how the VM is doing
$ lmx doctor       # what is wrong, and the fix
$ lmx help docker  # commands and tasks of a module

steps.title: From a file to a *running machine*
steps.lead: `limanix` is the only thing you install on the Mac.

items.title: Download
items.text: One binary for Apple Silicon and Intel Macs on macOS 26 or newer.

items.title: Create
items.text: Describe the machine in `limanix.toml` and build it.

items.title: Work in it
items.text: Open a shell, or [connect VS Code, Cursor, Zed or JetBrains](https://docs.limanix.dev/vms/editors) over SSH.

steps.note: Change the file later and run `limanix update`. The VM keeps running while the new system builds, and restarts into it only if the build succeeds.

catalog.title: A catalog that *fits together*
catalog.lead: Shell components, toolchains and services share one theme and know about each other. Anything else comes from nixpkgs.
catalog.hint: Pick a module to see what it works with.
catalog.about: Every module and tool in the catalog. A line joins two that work together: a language server reaches the editor, a key in one opens the other, one theme colors them all.
catalog.mapHint: Pick one to see what it works with. Drag to move around; pinch, or scroll with Ctrl held, to zoom.

items.question: Is LimaNix free?
items.answer: Yes. LimaNix is open source under the Apache License 2.0.

items.question: Do I need to know Nix?
items.answer: No. `limanix.toml` covers the shell, toolchains, modules and packages. When you need more, a NixOS module of your own plugs into the same VM.

items.question: How is it different from Lima?
items.answer: LimaNix runs its VMs with Lima, built into the `limanix` binary. On top it adds a NixOS system built from your file, a catalog of modules that work together, and updates that build before the VM restarts.

items.question: How is it different from OrbStack or Docker Desktop?
items.answer: They run containers well. LimaNix describes the whole development machine in `limanix.toml`: the shell, languages, services and packages, built the same way on every Mac. Containers run inside it too: add `lmx:docker` for Docker Engine with Compose.

items.question: Why not devcontainers, nix-darwin or devenv?
items.answer: Devcontainers run a project in a container and need a container runtime on the Mac. nix-darwin and devenv install Nix and your tools on macOS itself. LimaNix keeps all of it in a Linux VM, where Linux tools and services run as they do on a server, and the Mac needs only `limanix`.

items.question: Which Macs does it support?
items.answer: Apple Silicon and Intel Macs with macOS 26 or newer.

items.question: Where do my files live?
items.answer: Project folders stay on your Mac and are shared into the VM. Your home in the VM is stored on the Mac too: it survives updates and stays when you delete the VM.

closing.title: Your next Linux machine is one file away
